svg.text: PowerMonger economy: what moves a lord's food, men, goods and loyalty
Flows into and out of one lord record $4e514 (32 bytes); every flow is a write by a named routine
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990) is a war game on a height-mapped land of settlements. Each settlement belongs to a lord,
and each lord has a 32-byte record holding four things the player has to manage: his food store, his men at home, eight goods counters and
a loyalty pressure that turns the lord to another side when it reaches 600. The armies the player and the computer lords command are
captains' groups that take food, men and goods from their lords.
There is no economy routine that grows a population or balances food once per period. Every change to those four numbers is a single write
made by one man's state-machine handler (his "mode", written $xx) or by an order. The figure collects every such write for one lord
record: the civilians who fill it on the left, the record in the middle, the armies that draw on it on the right.

svg.text: How to read it
Middle: the lord record, one box per field, named by its byte offset in the record (+6 is byte 6). Left: civilian men in their job modes. Right: the
army, a captain's group record and its men. Each arrow is one kind of write: an arrow into the middle adds to the field, an arrow out of it subtracts,
a pair of arrows does both. The label on the arrow is the change per event; "slice" and ">> shift" are the posture-scaled amounts explained below. The
first line of each box names the event and the routine or mode that makes the write; the fill is the evidence for that flow.
What to take from it
Food. Food comes in only from fishermen (+4 a catch) and farmers coming home (+2). It leaves to armies, to gatherers whose delivery has no group, and
to the winter upkeep, one per parked man per pulse.
Men. Men are conserved: every arrow on the men field moves one man between the lord, a group or another lord, and none is born after the world build
(observed over traced runs, not proven absent). The pigeon landing is the one path that adds a man without taking him from elsewhere: it revives a
dead man's record.
Goods. Goods come in one at a time from felled trees, heavily throttled, and are spent by armies to equip and upgrade their men. What the game calls
invention is that upgrade, not a research timer. Men and goods are separate ledgers: goods never become men, and food and goods meet only in the
trade.
Loyalty. A lord's towns that go hungry in winter push his loyalty pressure up; at 600 he and his settlements change side and the pressure resets to
300. This is the game's own clock, not something the player triggers.
Terms and evidence
shift = posture - 2 ($30fe). Posture is the group's aggression setting (2, 3 or 4), and an order moves food >> shift: aggressive takes all, neutral
half, passive a quarter. 36(group) is the group's own food, which the captain panel labels "Food:". troops_field is the lord's men at home, not in an
army. The winter park (mode $7c) needs the season word $57fd0 == 0: farmers ($16), merchants ($4e) and fishers ($5e) park there, so upkeep and loyalty
move only in winter (a man idling in $7e pulses too, never on that first-pulse edge). Mission 1 builds both enemy lords at 608; the first winter pulse
resets them to 300.
Proven means a gate passed: a Python rewrite of the routine was run beside the game's own 68000 code from many saved states and every changed byte
matched (18452/18452 is matching bytes out of bytes compared). Gates: gate_fsm15.py (job modes, 18452/18452 bytes), gate_orders.py ($600a, $60dc,
$61f8, $6352, $638c, $63f4), gate_equip.py ($160f8, 385/385 over 201 states), diff_revolt.py (1778/1778 over 49 states), heartbeat block (99/99). Live
means seen running in the emulator and counted: "live: town 22 -> 11" is one run in which a town's food went from 22 to 11; "k5_s4, 100M" is a saved
state on land 5 run for 100 million emulated instructions. Code read means from the disassembly only.
Evidence:
proven (gate vs the real 68000)
live (seen running, counted)
